content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler Vegetable Puree, NFS (4875) is a ready‑to‑eat product designed for infants from 6 months old. It contains carefully selected vegetables steamed and blended to a smooth consistency, without added salt, sugar or preservatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The puree is made from fresh, pesticide‑free vegetables.
Ingredients include carrot, pumpkin, broccoli and sweet potato – rich sources of vitamins A, C and K.
Steam processing retains up to 90 % of the nutrients.
The product meets strict NFS (National Food Safety) quality standards.
Packaged in BPA‑free, microwave‑safe plastic.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and C
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and immunity, while vitamin C provides antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and a balanced gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low in sodium
items.content: No added salt makes the puree gentle on a baby’s kidneys.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The smooth texture and lack of lumps aid digestion in young children.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: While vegetables rarely cause allergies, monitor the infant during the first introduction.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: In some regions nitrate levels can be higher; the product is tested to meet safety limits.

items.title: Not suitable for children over 12 months without pediatric advice
items.content: After 12 months, a more varied texture and flavor profile may be needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree straight from the pouch, gently warming it in the microwave (30‑40 seconds). For a thinner consistency, add a little breast milk or infant formula.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the unopened pouch in a cool, dry place until the ‘best before’ date. Once opened, refrigerate at +4 °C and use within 24 hours.

chiles-rellenos-filled-with-meat-and-che.title: Chiles rellenos with meat and cheese

content.title: About
content.content: Chiles rellenos is a classic Mexican dish consisting of large peppers stuffed with a mixture of ground meat and cheese, then baked in a tomato‑based sauce with spices. The peppers are usually poblano or jalapeño that have been blanched, and the filling can include beef, pork, or a blend, along with a melting cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the colonial era when Spanish settlers introduced cheese and meat to native Mexican cuisine.
There are many filling variations, from traditional beef to chicken, turkey, or even seafood.
Chiles rellenos are often served with a tomato sauce, green chile sauce, or a creamy sauce, depending on the region.
Some regions use sweet bell peppers to balance the heat of the filling.
The dish is commonly prepared for holidays and family celebrations as a hearty, festive meal.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and cheese contain B1, B2, B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Vitamin C from peppers
items.content: Fresh peppers are high in vitamin C, boosting immunity and aiding iron absorption.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Peppers provide carotenoids and other antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Pepper heat
items.content: Some pepper varieties can be very hot; people with sensitive stomachs should choose milder types.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and meat can contain saturated fats, so moderation is recommended.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should use dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese and prepared sauces often contain salt; those with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Remove seeds from the peppers and lightly sauté them until tender. Stuff with a mixture of ground meat, spices, and grated cheese. Close the peppers, bake at 180 °C (350 °F) for 25‑30 minutes until the cheese melts and browns. Serve with tomato sauce or fresh salsa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cooked chiles rellenos can be kept in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg yolk is the yellow part of a chicken egg that contains almost all of the egg’s nutrients: fats, proteins, vitamins, and minerals. Raw yolk is commonly used in cooking for sauces, desserts, and as a nutrient‑dense ingredient.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The yolk holds nearly all of the egg’s vitamins B, as well as vitamins A, D, E, and K.
About 55 % of an egg’s calories are found in the yolk.
Yolk color varies with the hen’s diet; more carotenoids produce a deeper yellow.
Raw yolk is a key ingredient in classic sauces such as hollandaise, mayonnaise, and certain custards.
Yolks contain lecithin, a natural emulsifier that helps blend fats and water.

items.title: Rich in vitamins A and D
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and immunity, while vitamin D is essential for bone health and immune function.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Yolk proteins contain all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains lecithin
items.content: Lecithin aids liver function and promotes normal fat metabolism.

items.title: Mineral dense
items.content: Yolks provide iron, phosphorus, calcium, and zinc, supporting blood formation, bone strength, and immune health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Vitamin E and carotenoids in yolk protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Raw yolk can be contaminated with Salmonella bacteria, so people with weakened immunity, pregnant women, and young children should prefer cooked eggs.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: A single yolk contains about 186 mg of cholesterol, which may be a concern for cholesterol‑restricted diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to yolk, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw yolk can be whisked into sauces (hollandaise, mayonnaise), added to smoothies, used in desserts (mousses, custards), or incorporated into baked goods. When consuming raw, ensure eggs are fresh and sourced from reputable suppliers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep eggs refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Use raw yolk within 2‑3 days after separating from the white. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Milk is a nutrient-rich liquid produced by mammals to feed their young and is a staple food in many cultures. Cow's milk is the most common, though milk from goats, sheep, buffalo, and camels is also consumed. It is drunk on its own, added to tea, coffee, and cereal, and used to make yogurt, cheese, butter, and many other dairy products.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Milk is typically pasteurized, a heat treatment named after Louis Pasteur that reduces harmful bacteria.
Milk is sold with different fat contents, such as skim, low-fat, and whole.
Most milk is homogenized so that the fat does not separate and rise to the top.
Milk is the base for yogurt, cheese, kefir, butter, and cottage cheese.
Many people worldwide lose some ability to digest lactose after childhood.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Milk is a well-known source of calcium, which supports healthy bones and teeth.

items.title: Provides high-quality protein
items.content: Milk contains casein and whey proteins that include all essential amino acids.

items.title: Contains B vitamins
items.content: Milk provides vitamin B12 and riboflavin (B2), which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Often fortified with vitamin D
items.content: Many types of milk have added vitamin D, which supports calcium absorption.

items.title: Provides potassium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals support normal muscle and bone function.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Cow's milk protein allergy is among the more common food allergies, especially in young children.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after drinking milk. Lactose-free milk is an alternative.

items.title: Raw milk
items.content: Unpasteurized milk can carry harmful bacteria and is not recommended, especially for children, pregnant women, and older adults.

items.title: Infants and medication interactions
items.content: Cow's milk should not replace breast milk or formula as the main drink for infants under one year. Calcium in milk can reduce the absorption of some medicines, such as certain antibiotics, so follow the instructions from your doctor or pharmacist.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Milk can be drunk on its own, warmed, or added to coffee, tea, porridge, cereal, and smoothies. It is used in cooking and baking, in soups and sauces, and in puddings and desserts. It can also be turned into yogurt and other fermented dairy products.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep milk refrigerated at or below about 4 °C (40 °F) and return it to the refrigerator soon after pouring. Use it by the date on the package and within a few days after opening, and do not use milk that smells or tastes sour. Unopened ultra-pasteurized (UHT) milk can be stored at room temperature until opened. Freezing may change the texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork hash is a ready‑to‑eat mixture of finely chopped boiled or stewed pork, potatoes, onions and spices. It is often used as a quick side dish or main course that can be reheated on a skillet or in the microwave.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of making hash originated in Europe in the 19th century as a way to use leftover meat.
Pork hash is commonly served with fried eggs or sauerkraut.
In some regions the hash is enriched with tomato paste or sweet bell pepper for a brighter flavor.
Hash stores well in the refrigerator for up to 5 days and can be frozen for up to 3 months.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pork provides a high‑quality source of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The iron in pork is highly bioavailable and helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hash supplies vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of zinc
items.content: Zinc contributes to immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Pork can be fatty, so people watching calorie intake should control portion sizes.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Prepared hash often contains added salt and food preservatives; those with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to salmonella or campylobacter contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the hash in a skillet with a little oil until golden brown, serve with a green salad, sauerkraut or a fried egg. Fresh herbs such as parsley or dill add extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared hash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 5 days. For longer storage freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat thoroughly to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

rice-brown-with-peas-and-carrots-ns-as-t.title: Brown Rice with Peas and Carrots

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with peas and carrots is a ready‑to‑eat product that combines whole‑grain brown rice, green peas and carrots. It is rich in fiber, B‑vitamins, vitamin A and minerals, and provides a slow‑release source of energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains the bran and germ, making it more nutritious than white rice.
Peas are a good source of plant protein and phytonutrients that support muscle growth.
Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The combination offers a balanced mix of carbs, protein and vitamins in one dish.
The product is often used in children’s meals and weight‑management diets.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of plant protein
items.content: Peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g of product, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Vitamin A from carrots
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immune function and skin health.

items.title: Minerals and B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice supplies magnesium, phosphorus and vitamins B1, B3, B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Brown rice raises blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: The bran of brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

items.title: Arsenic presence
items.content: Like most rice, brown rice may contain trace amounts of inorganic arsenic; a varied diet is recommended.

items.title: Digestive load
items.content: High fiber amounts can cause gastrointestinal discomfort for people with sensitive stomachs when eaten in large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to heat: microwave or stir‑fry for 2–3 minutes, then season to taste. Serve as a side dish, add to salads, pack in lunch boxes, or use as a base for vegetarian meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed container. After opening, consume within 4–6 weeks. Discard if you notice moldy odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Gazpacho is a cold Spanish soup made from fresh vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers, bell peppers, onion, and garlic, seasoned with olive oil, vinegar, and spices. Served chilled, it offers a bright flavor and refreshing aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gazpacho originated in Andalusia in the 19th century as a way to use surplus summer vegetables.
Traditional recipes do not include bread, though some variations add stale bread for thickness.
There are many regional versions, including cucumber gazpacho and watermelon gazpacho.
The original recipe used wine vinegar; today apple or balsamic vinegar is common.
Gazpacho is often garnished with diced vegetables and croutons for textural contrast.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and peppers provide lycopene and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The high water and vegetable content makes it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: Served cold with a high water content, it helps maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil adds monounsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The vegetables supply dietary fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or other ingredients.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Adding too much salt or using ready‑made sauces can increase sodium load on the kidneys.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Vinegar and tomatoes make the soup acidic; people with gastritis or reflux should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gazpacho chilled in bowls or glasses, often topped with finely diced vegetables, herbs, croutons, or a drizzle of olive oil. It can be enjoyed as a light snack, a starter, or a refreshing lunch on hot days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep gazpacho in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Stir well before serving, as ingredients may settle. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size containers, though texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Sunflower seeds are the edible seeds of the sunflower (Helianthus annuus). They are offered in two versions: plain and lightly salted. They have a mild nutty flavor, a crunchy texture, and can be enjoyed as a snack or used as an ingredient in various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sunflower is one of the world’s most cultivated crops, and its seeds are a major source of vegetable oil.
Sunflower seeds are rich in vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant.
There are more than 70 sunflower varieties, differing in size and oil content.
The seeds can be processed into tahini paste and are used in baking.
A field of sunflowers is often seen as a symbol of happiness and energy.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E protects cells from oxidative stress and supports skin health.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat is polyunsaturated, including omega‑6 fatty acids, which are important for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium is essential for muscle and nerve function and energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Seeds supply plant protein and dietary fiber, promoting satiety and healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains phytosterols
items.content: Phytosterols may help lower blood cholesterol levels.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to sunflower seeds.

items.title: High sodium in salted versions
items.content: Excessive salt intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Seeds are calorie‑dense, so they should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Potential contaminants
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth and aflatoxin formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sunflower seeds can be eaten straight from the bag, added to salads, yogurt, granola, baked goods, or used in sauces and spreads. The salted version adds a savory note, but for lower sodium choose the plain variety.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard seeds that smell rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Tea, bubble is a beverage that combines traditional brewed tea with small flavored popping pearls, similar to tapioca balls. The pearls are usually made from gelatin or plant‑based alternatives and are filled with fruit syrup, giving the drink a sweet taste and a fun texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first versions appeared in Taiwan in the early 2000s and quickly spread across Asia.
Popping pearls come in many flavors: mango, strawberry, passion fruit, mint, and more.
In some countries the pearls are made without gelatin, making the drink suitable for vegetarians and vegans.
Bubble tea is often served cold over ice, but it can also be enjoyed hot.
Pearl size typically ranges from 2–5 mm, allowing them to melt gently in the mouth and release their syrup.

items.title: Tea antioxidants
items.content: Black and green teas used in the drink are rich in polyphenols, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The beverage is mostly water, contributing to the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Vitamins from fruit syrups
items.content: The syrups inside the pearls can provide vitamin C and small amounts of B‑vitamins.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Fragrant fruit notes and sweetness can stimulate serotonin production, improving mood.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Warm tea can relax the stomach and support digestion.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit syrups in the pearls can be very sweet, increasing the drink’s calorie load.

items.title: Gelatin allergy
items.content: Traditional pearls contain gelatin, which may cause allergic reactions in some individuals.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Consuming a large number of pearls may cause stomach upset or diarrhea in sensitive people.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Fruit additives can raise the drink’s acidity, which may be problematic for those with reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve bubble tea cold over ice or hot, adding the pearls directly to the glass before serving. Stir gently so the pearls distribute evenly, then enjoy the aromatic flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared tea in a sealed container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store the pearls in a dry, airtight bag at room temperature to prevent them from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Vienna sausage, canned, is a ready‑to‑eat meat product made from finely ground pork and beef, seasoned with spices and flavorings. It is packed in a hermetically sealed metal can, providing a long shelf life without refrigeration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Vienna sausage was created in Austria at the end of the 19th century as a convenient snack for travelers.
Traditional recipes combine beef, pork, onion, salt, white pepper and paprika.
Cans are often coated with a lacquer layer to prevent corrosion and preserve flavor.
Vienna sausage is popular in many post‑Soviet countries, where it is used in salads, sandwiches and hot dishes.
There are nitrite‑free versions aimed at consumers who avoid artificial preservatives.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The sausage provides about 12–14 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Typically less than 2 g of carbs per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Convenient and long‑lasting
items.content: The sealed can allows storage for 2–3 years without refrigeration.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Vienna sausage is fairly salty (about 1.5 g of salt per 100 g), so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some varieties contain nitrites, which may cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Contains 20–25 g of fat per 100 g, including saturated fatty acids.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to pork or beef may experience reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sausage can be eaten straight from the can, warmed in the microwave or skillet, added to salads, pasta, omelets, or used as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–5 days.
